newsitem.title: JAPAN: Generous BOJ moves may reflect DKB woes - bankers.
newsitem.headline: Generous BOJ moves may reflect DKB woes - bankers.

text.p: The rising woes of scandal-ridden Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) may be a major factor behind the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) recent generous supply of funds to the market, money traders said on Wednesday.

In a surprise move, the BOJ placed the market in surplus to the tune of 300 billion yen on Wednesday via accommodative operations. The central bank has already been unusually generous by letting the market maintain a surplus of some 200 billion yen since the start of this week.

"Last week, DKB was seen taking funds with a one-month term. But this week they appear to be taking funds with one-, two- and three-month terms, in both the Euroyen and domestic yen interest rate markets, and this is putting short-term interest rates under pressure across the board," said Shin Nagai, money market manager at ABN Amro Bank.
These actions are widely perceived by the market as a pre-emptive move by DKB to secure sufficient funds to meet its needs should it become unable to do so in the future.
There were rumours in the market on Tuesday that DKB might face suspension from taking part in BOJ market operations, although a BOJ official later denied this.

"Despite the BOJ's denial, the threat still hangs over DKB, forcing them into the longer-term market. And although there are no reasons now why they cannot take funds, you sense a certain fear on their part," one trader said.
These fears are spurring DKB to take in longer-term funds at higher rates, forcing other banks to follow, traders said.
The three-month Euroyen interest rate rose to 0.625 percent on Wednesday, up from around 0.600 percent a week ago.
The banks' moves are helping to push up the overnight rate by convincing market players that longer-term rates have the potential to rise even higher.
The key overnight rate continued to cling stubbornly just below 0.5 percent on Wednesday despite the BOJ's efforts to alleviate the upward pressure.
"Unless the BOJ continues its accommodative moves, probably on today's scale, we may well see the overnight rate rise again for the rest of this week," one trader said.

But a city bank trader warned, and other dealers agreed, that it is far too simple to blame everything on DKB, noting that the approaching end of the bank reporting period and the high volume of certificates of deposit maturing this month are also playing a part. Traders said that as much as 19 trillion yen worth of CDs will be maturing this month.
On Tuesday, four former DKB executives were arrested by Tokyo prosecutors on suspicion of violating the Commercial Code.

The followed the arrest last Thursday of four other DKB officials on suspicion of extending massive uncollateralised loans to Ryuichi Koike, the racketeer at the centre of a scandal which has also embroiled Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
